method: Direct header and class-test audit; no C++ build or execution. The header is inline-only and has no .cpp.
evidence_tier: tier 3 (source review, transcribed class-test literals) and tier 4 (independently derived lexical cases and native bounds)

source_anchors.operation: basename returns file.substr(file.find_last_of("\\/") + 1); the header's own comment records that it preserves File::basename's unsigned npos + 1 wraparound to zero, which is what makes a separator-free path return itself
to_path constructs std::filesystem::path from std::u8string because the std::string constructor uses the active Windows code page rather than UTF-8
Windows-only catch of std::system_error falls back to the ANSI code-page constructor for bytes that are not valid UTF-8, for example an argv filename
single class-test section: byte-exact u8string round trip for ASCII, U+00E4, CJK, embedded spaces, a 300-character name and mixed CJK plus diacritics

class_test_review.literal_extraction: All six cross-platform round-trip literals are transcribed into tests/path_utils.rs. The three _WIN32-only cases (PathUtils_test.cpp:74-127) are not ported: two of them exercise the ANSI fallback for the byte 0xE4, which a Rust &str cannot represent - once on a bare filename and once inside a UNC path - and the third is a plain ASCII UNC path that the port accepts with no special handling.

native_boundaries: basename delegates to system::file::basename rather than duplicating the source's second copy of File::basename
to_path returns Result and refuses a path above 1 MiB or containing NUL; the source checks neither
The source's Windows ANSI fallback is unreachable: a Rust &str is valid UTF-8 by construction and PathBuf stores it losslessly on every platform
Both entry points stay purely lexical: no filesystem access, no normalisation of dot segments or repeated separators, no symlink resolution
